variantDescriptions.base: retronym/scala#212 head plus scala/scala#11381 (`claude/closed-scope-bench-base`) + retronym/scala#243 (TypeRef fold: `NonClassTypeRef` an abstract class), branch `claude/typeref-bench-base`
variantDescriptions.fast2: `fast1` plus the `Made` bit: no table lookups for a closed scope until it has handed out a type not in the table (`claude/closed-scope-fastpath-bench`) + retronym/scala#243 (TypeRef fold: `NonClassTypeRef` an abstract class), branch `claude/typeref-bench-fast2`
variantDescriptions.loose: `fast2` loosened (option D): a closed scope only keeps the types it makes out of the uniques table. No suspension for caches, no interning of `TypeVar` bounds and instances, no `Made` bit, no `hasPartOutsideTable`/`isEntry`, no watermark; completions still run outside the scope. A type made in a scope may outlive it, equal to but not the table's instance. Branch `claude/typeref-bench-loose`

name: m4-closed-loose-kperf
description: Spike of the loose closed scope (option D) against base and fast2, all with retronym/scala#243. Does dropping the bookkeeping that keeps escaping types interned make closed scopes cheaper than base, or does lost sharing (recomputed per-instance caches) cost more? PMU profile, kperf, one fork per variant, 15 + 3 single shots, typer only. Not a timing A/B.
